\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, proportionally}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact; from $k\!=\!6$ the panel splits.
Pooled at $k\ge6$, repeated items are rendered with a median error of
\ErrRep{}\% $[\ErrRepLo{}, \ErrRepHi{}]$ ($n=\ErrRepN{}$), one-directional:
models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than requested, never systematically
more.

Within $k\le32$, though, the deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating ---
not what Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iv) predicts. A constant fits the panel's
median count above $k\!=\!6$ with residual sum of squares \ShapeSatSSE{} against
\ShapePropSSE{} for $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$, in \ShapePropModels{} of
\ErrNModels{} checkpoints (S10). A finite $N^\ast$ implies the count levels off;
here it tracks the request, so the horizon is not inside this ladder.

\subsection{Past the ladder, the count does level off}

So we extended it to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ on the carriers common to both
(S10). Tracking stops: the repeated median \emph{falls} from \HzMedRepKLo{} at
$k\!=\!48$ to \HzMedRepKHi{} at $k\!=\!128$ as the request grows threefold.

The controls stop us reading this as counting collapse alone: they saturate too,
near \HzMedCtlKHi{} units, so these decoders have a general utterance-length
ceiling and the reportable quantity is the \emph{ratio}, which divides it out.
Fitting $\hat c(k)=N^\ast(1-e^{-k/N^\ast})$ over the combined ladder gives
$N^\ast_{\mathrm{rep}}=\HzNRep{}$ $[\HzNRepLo{},\HzNRepHi{}]$ against
$N^\ast_{\mathrm{ctl}}=\HzNCtl{}$ $[\HzNCtlLo{},\HzNCtlHi{}]$, disjoint in
\HzNSep{} of \HzNModels{} checkpoints: repetition lowers the counting horizon
\HzRatio{}-fold. That is the theorem's consequence, just past where our original
ladder stopped --- which is why $k\le32$ looked proportional.

Two things keep this short of clean confirmation: the extension covers
\HzNModels{} checkpoints with few items per cell, and a pure horizon predicts a
plateau whereas the repeated median \emph{declines}
(\HzDeclinePeak{}$\rightarrow$\HzDeclineLast{}). The judge's bias points the same
way (S9), making \HzRatio{} an upper bound.

What degrades with $k$ is reliability rather than proportion: the share rendered
\emph{exactly} right falls from \ExactRepKLo{}\% at $k\!=\!\ExactRepKLoVal{}$ to
\ExactRepKHi{}\% at $k\!=\!\ExactRepKHiVal{}$. The effect separates from its own
control in \ErrNSep{} of \ErrNModels{} checkpoints --- \ErrBestModel{} shows no
deficit at all --- and holds whether the repeated unit is a word, a sentence or a
place-value pattern.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control has its
twin's carrier and word count, differing only in that the $k$ copies of one word
become $k$ non-adjacent ones. Were the failure about sequence length, attention span
or exposure bias, the curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$ the median
control error is \ErrCtl{}\% $[\ErrCtlLo{}, \ErrCtlHi{}]$ over $n=\ErrCtlN{}$
generations, at every $k$ up to $32$, for every model. The contrast is sharpest
in exactly-correct renderings --- \ExactCtl{}\% for controls against
\ExactRep{}\% for their twins: decoders that miscount a repeated sequence five
times in six render its non-adjacent twin correctly nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- the residual \CtlMissPct{}\% carry
genuine truncations --- but they are exact where the repeated items are not.

Two rival explanations --- that repeated text is simply improbable, and that the
attractor is acoustic rather than text-side --- are ruled out by their own
predictions (S8).

\subsection{The decoder buys states more slowly under repetition}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says states visited under periodic conditioning
stop being mutually distinguishable, so more repetitions should buy distinct
internal states more slowly than the same amount of non-repetitive text does. We
count states by the effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp(-\sum_i p_i
\log p_i)$ of the trajectory over normalised singular values; the statistic is
the \emph{capacity gain}
$\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$, bootstrapped over
templates.

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c,d) shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain, with disjoint 95\% intervals for
\CapSepPhrase{} panel checkpoints; the matched-pair form of
the comparison gives a positive gap in \CapFracPos{}\% of pairs.

An obvious objection is circularity: rendering \emph{very} sixteen times really
does produce monotonous audio, so a low-rank trajectory might follow from the
stimulus rather than from lost capacity. It does not. Adding realised output
diversity (type/token ratio, adjacent-repeat rate, length) as covariates leaves
the ratio at \CapAdjRatio{}; restricting to correctly rendered items leaves it at
\CapCorrRatio{}. The gain stays \emph{positive} in \CapPosModels{} of
\ErrNModels{} checkpoints, so at $k\le32$ repetition slows state acquisition
without halting it --- consistent with decoders below their horizon rather than
at it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} concerns the softmax \emph{restricted to the $k$
repeated keys}. Renormalised over those columns, profile entropy grows with
$\log k$ at slope \BlockEntropySlope{} and the most-attended occurrence holds
$\ShareMedK{}/k$ of the block's mass typically, $\ShareMaxK{}/k$ at worst: the
extreme spread Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} needs is $\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$
nats, so attention is near-uniform typically but not uniformly so (S4).
Qwen3-TTS sums text and acoustic embeddings per position, so the lemma cannot be
checked there.
